subject: Architecture
title: Mud Brick: The First Building Material
description: A quick, practical guide to Mud Brick: The First Building Material.

hook.text: The oldest known bricks are 11,000 years old, found in the Jordan Valley.

buildup.text: Early builders mixed mud with straw and dried it in the sun. No kiln needed.

discovery.text: Mud brick let humans build permanent walls, rooms, and multi-story structures.

twist.text: The material is still used today. A third of the world's population lives in earthen buildings.

climax.text: Adobe, cob, and rammed earth are all variations of the same ancient idea.

punchline.text: Dirt and water built civilizations. They still do.

quiz.question: What fraction of the world's population lives in earthen buildings?

details.summary: Mud brick — sun-dried clay mixed with straw — is humanity's oldest manufactured building material, used continuously for over 10,000 years. Cities like Çatalhöyük and Jericho were built entirely of mud brick, and the material still houses billions of people across Africa, Asia.
details.whyItMatters: Mud brick demonstrates that great architecture doesn't require industrial materials. The world's cheapest and most accessible building material has housed more humans across history than any other.
takeaways: Humanity's oldest manufactured building material at 10,000+ years
Sun-dried clay and straw built the first cities
Still houses billions of people across three continents today

faq.question: How are mud bricks made?
faq.answer: Clay soil is mixed with water and straw binder, pressed into wooden molds, and dried in the sun for several days. The straw provides tensile reinforcement similar to rebar in concrete. Once dry, bricks are strong enough for multi-story construction and last decades with proper roof protection.

faq.question: Why is straw added to mud bricks?
faq.answer: Straw fibers prevent cracking as the brick dries and shrinks. They also add tensile strength, since dried clay is strong in compression but weak in tension. The straw functions exactly like fiberglass in modern composites — reinforcing a brittle matrix material with flexible fibers.
